enonce_markdown: Which observation on a hillside is the best evidence of soil creep?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Match each landform to its process: creep is very slow, continuous and visible only through tilted objects; the other forms are the products of rapid movements.

### Solution

Creep is a slow downslope movement of soil, too slow to see, caused by repeated expansion and contraction. Its signs are leaning poles and posts and trees curving at the base. A curved scar with hummocky ground below it is a slump, the mud tongue with raised banks is a mudflow, and the pile of boulders is a rockfall talus.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: A pile of angular boulders at the bottom of a vertical rock face
Fence posts and utility poles leaning downslope and tree trunks curved at the base
A narrow tongue of wet mud with raised side banks reaching the valley floor
A curved scar at the top of a slope with a hummocky mass of soil at the foot

enonce_markdown: A landslide happens when, along a potential failure surface,
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A slope is stable while the resisting force (shear strength) exceeds the driving force (shear stress); failure starts when this is reversed.

### Solution

Gravity produces a shear stress that drives material downslope, and the friction and cohesion of the material give a shear strength which resists it. When the driving shear stress exceeds the resisting strength, the mass moves. The other statements describe a stable slope or are irrelevant.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the normal stress is zero because the slope is vertical
the shear strength becomes greater than the shear stress
the shear stress becomes greater than the shear strength of the material
the water table falls below the base of the slope

enonce_markdown: Why do many landslides in hilly regions happen during or just after a period of very heavy rain?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Shear strength depends on the effective normal stress, which is the total normal stress minus the pore-water pressure.

### Solution

In saturated material the water supports part of the load, so the effective normal stress falls and the friction that resists sliding decreases. The extra weight of water also adds to the shear stress, but the main trigger is the loss of strength through higher pore pressure. Swelling clays lose strength rather than gain it, and flattening a slope would reduce the downslope stress, not increase it.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Water raises the pore-water pressure, which lowers the effective normal stress and so the frictional shear strength of the slope material
Rain increases the cohesion of clay minerals by making them swell
Water only adds weight to the slope, while the shear strength of the material is not changed
Rain flattens the slope by erosion, which increases the downslope shear stress

enonce_markdown: A block of sandstone 40 m long slides on a smooth bedding plane that dips at 20 degrees in the same direction as the slope, and it stays almost intact as it moves. Which type of movement is this?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The shape of the failure surface identifies the type of slide: planar surfaces control translational slides, curved concave surfaces control rotational slides.

### Solution

The block moves along a flat, pre-existing weakness (the bedding plane), so it is a **translational slide**. A rotational slump moves on a curved, spoon-shaped surface in homogeneous soft material, a rockfall is a free fall or bouncing of detached blocks from a steep face, and creep is a very slow movement of soil.

**Answer: C.**

enonce_markdown:
For a dry slope of cohesionless material, the factor of safety against sliding is given by $FS = \tan\varphi / \tan\beta$, where $\varphi$ is the angle of internal friction of the material and $\beta$ the slope angle. A road builder is cutting through weathered sand with $\varphi = 35^\circ$.

(a) Calculate FS for a slope cut at $28^\circ$ and state whether it is stable.

(b) The cut is made steeper, at $38^\circ$. Calculate the new FS and state what is expected to happen.

(c) Give two measures that could stabilise a slope cut steeper than the angle of internal friction.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The slope is stable if the resisting forces exceed the driving forces, that is if FS > 1; it fails if FS < 1.

### Solution

(a) $FS = \tan 35^\circ / \tan 28^\circ = 0.7002 / 0.5317 = 1.32$. Since FS > 1 the slope is stable.

(b) $FS = \tan 35^\circ / \tan 38^\circ = 0.7002 / 0.7813 = 0.90$. Since FS < 1 the cut is steeper than the angle of friction, so the sand will slide until a slope of about $35^\circ$ is reached.

(c) Any two of: retaining wall or gabions at the toe, rock bolts or soil nails, drainage to lower the pore-water pressure, benching or terracing, vegetation whose roots bind the soil.

enonce_markdown:
A new road is cut at the foot of a 30 degree hillside of deeply weathered granite (a clay-rich saprolite) near Bamenda. The hillside was cleared of forest for farming and houses stand near the top. Several landslides occurred during the last rainy season.

(a) Explain how each of the following increases the risk of failure: (i) the road cut at the toe, (ii) the removal of the forest, (iii) the heavy seasonal rainfall.

(b) Propose three measures to reduce the risk, and explain how each acts on the stresses or strengths involved.

(c) Why is public education still an essential part of reducing the impacts of landslides in such an area?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Always link a cause to its effect on either the driving stress (weight, steepness, load) or the resisting strength (friction, cohesion, pore pressure, root reinforcement).

### Solution

(a) (i) The cut removes the support at the toe and makes the slope steeper, so the shear stress rises and the buttressing material is lost. (ii) Without trees there are no roots to bind the soil and no interception or uptake of water, so cohesion falls and more water infiltrates. (iii) Heavy rain saturates the saprolite, raising the pore-water pressure and cutting the effective normal stress, which reduces friction, while the water also adds to the weight of the slope.

(b) Any three of: **drainage** (surface ditches and sub-surface drains) to lower the pore pressure and raise strength; **retaining wall or gabions** at the toe to restore the support lost by the cut; **re-grading and benching** to reduce the angle and the load at the head; **replanting** deep-rooted trees and grass to bind the soil and take up water; **no building** near the top of the slope to remove the extra load.

(c) Engineering works are costly and cannot cover every slope, so people must know the warning signs (cracks, leaning trees, springs, muddy water), avoid building on unstable slopes and know how to react in heavy rain. Education lowers losses everywhere.
